They offered Enron an opportunity to invest in a patented method of generating electricity by converting methane to hydrogen and burning hydrogen in a high efficiency turbine. This patent represents an idea, without any exhaustive quantitative analysis or research and without any prototype demonstrated in the field or a lab.We politely told Mr. Hatchett that we would review his proposal and get back to him.Subsequently, we conveyed to Mr. Hatchett that a) methane consumption rate for an integrated facility based on the subject patent is higher than the conventional plant efficiency b) the result in fuel cost is higher c) the overall Co2 emissions are probably higher d) there is no economical or technical justification to support an investment of Enron funds. We informed Bob Hatchett that we would recommend to Enron that Enron not invest in the development of this effort. While we invited Mr. Hatchett to respond back to us regarding our analysis, I see no further action required by us at this time.Please let me know if you want us to draft anything from you to Mr. Hatchett regarding this subject.LI39200
col3: As requested, my team and I held a meeting with Robert Hatchett and his colleagues. They presented Enron with an investment opportunity in a patented process for producing electricity through methane conversion to hydrogen, which is then used in a high-efficiency turbine. This patent is conceptual, lacking thorough quantitative analysis, research, or any prototype tested in a lab or real-world setting. We courteously informed Mr. Hatchett that we would evaluate his proposal and follow up. Later, we communicated to him that a) the methane usage for a facility using this patent exceeds conventional plant efficiency, b) fuel costs are consequently greater, c) total Co2 emissions are likely increased, and d) there is no economic or technical basis to justify an Enron investment. We told Bob Hatchett we would advise Enron against funding this development. Although we asked Mr. Hatchett to reply to our assessment, I believe no further steps are needed from us now. Please advise if you would like us to prepare any correspondence from you to Mr. Hatchett on this matter. LI39200

Here's your daily hook em.com update...Backup quarterback departing Texas  
Associated Press  
Posted: April 26, 2000  
AUSTIN — Adam Hall, the Texas Longhorns' backup quarterback in spring practice, will transfer from the University of Texas this fall, coach Mack Brown stated Wednesday.  

"The main reason is I want an opportunity to start soon," said Adam Hall, a redshirt freshman from Westlake High School.  

The university has granted Hall a release from his scholarship. He intends to finish the spring term and then enroll at another school in the fall. The new school was not identified in the announcement.  

"I care for all my teammates and am grateful for everything the coaches and staff have done for me at Texas, but I believe I'll have a better chance to play earlier elsewhere," he said.  

Hall went 4-for-5 for 85 yards and a touchdown in Texas' spring game on April 1. At Westlake in 1998, he completed 143 of 263 passes for 2,188 yards and 21 touchdowns.  

Brown described Hall as a diligent young man both on the field and academically. He wished the 6-foot-2, 205-pound quarterback well at his next stop.  

"Naturally we are very disappointed because we thought Adam had a good spring and were happy with his development," Brown said.  

I'll call you when I'm home tonight (around 6).  
Love you,  
Jenn

Paul: Here's more information regarding the "curtailment" data we are compiling.  
Utility Pricing for Core Gas Customers  
Before the relevant month, the utility projects gas prices using NYMEX monthly rates. For instance, based on November's projection, the utility determines the prices that core customers will pay in December.  
Once December ends, the utility evaluates the forecasted prices against the actual prices. If the forecast was too low, resulting in an undercollection, the utility will raise January's price projection by just the amount needed to offset the December shortfall. If prices were overestimated and there is an overcollection, the utility will lower January's price projection by exactly the sum required to return the excess.  
When the overcollection or undercollection is substantial, utilities typically distribute the adjustment across multiple months to prevent significant rate fluctuations in either direction. Yet, given the current situation, utilities might be less inclined to spread it out and could aim to recoup the full undercollection in the subsequent month. In summary, customer prices incorporate at least a one-month delay to accommodate discrepancies between forecasts and actual outcomes.

Canadian Privacy Law  
A major problem for companies that have offices in both Canada and the US is navigating the messy overlap between privacy regulations. Unlike the US’s patchwork of state laws (looking at you, CCPA and Virginia CDPA), Canada operates under PIPEDA—a federal law with teeth. Add in provincial rules like Quebec’s Law 25 or BC’s PIPA, and things get complicated fast. For multinationals, this means juggling consent requirements, data localization rules, and breach notification timelines that don’t always align. One misstep can mean fines, reputational damage, or worse—losing customer trust. That’s why smart companies invest early in cross-border compliance strategies and privacy-by-design frameworks.  

fyi,  
Dave  
Dave Cullinane, CPP, CIPP/US
col3:
Navigating Canadian Privacy Law  
For companies operating across Canada and the US, managing the complex interplay of privacy rules is a significant challenge. While the US relies on a mix of state regulations (such as the CCPA and Virginia CDPA), Canada follows the federal PIPEDA, which carries substantial enforcement power. This is further complicated by provincial legislation like Quebec’s Law 25 and British Columbia’s PIPA. Multinationals must balance differing standards for consent, data storage, and breach reporting, which often conflict. Errors can lead to penalties, harm to reputation, or—more critically—a loss of consumer confidence. Consequently, forward-thinking organizations prioritize developing cross-border compliance plans and integrating privacy from the outset.  

fyi,  
Dave  
Dave Cullinane, CPP, CIPP/US

A few thoughts:  

1. Section 2.1 (y) – the .30% should specify *per annum*. Right now, it’s ambiguous whether that’s a monthly, quarterly, or annual rate, and that could cause confusion (or worse, disputes) down the line. Better to be crystal clear.  

2. Section 4.3 – the cure period for defaults feels a bit tight at just five business days. Especially for payment-related hiccups, which can sometimes stem from administrative delays rather than actual financial trouble. Maybe bump it to ten? Gives everyone a little breathing room without compromising lender protections.  

3. Also, in the definitions section, “Material Adverse Effect” is pretty standard, but it might help to add a carve-out for general market downturns—otherwise, a broad economic dip could accidentally trigger a default.  

Overall, solid draft! Just a few tweaks for clarity and fairness would go a long way.

Below is a spreadsheet containing my preliminary estimate of the credit support value for MG and PaperCo. My methodology is outlined below:

1. Model all contracts as financial swaps.
2. Distribute the notional trading volumes across the estimated swap tenors.
3. Compute the default option value for each swap period using Black’s formula.
4. Treat these default option values as risky cash flows, similar to an annuity stream. By discounting this cash flow stream at both the original risky rate and the reduced-risk rate, I derive the credit enhancement value from the difference in the two NPVs.

col3: News: FERC Greenlights Independence and SupplyLink Projects 2:00 PM (CST) Jul 12, 2000 Following the submission of evidence demonstrating market demand through newly executed precedent agreements for firm transportation capacity, the heavily debated Independence Pipeline and associated SupplyLink pipeline initiatives received approval from FERC this morning. These projects had been under review at FERC for over three years. The FERC ruling enables the development of more than 900 MMcf/d of additional natural gas transport capacity between Chicago and Pennsylvania's Leidy Hub. A "tentative" operational target for the projects is set for November 2002. Their downstream counterpart, MarketLink, which gained FERC approval in April, is anticipated to commence operations a year earlier, according to a Williams Cos. spokesperson. Williams, Coastal, and National Fuel are backing the three pipeline ventures, collectively involving an investment of approximately $1.5 billion. The Commission authorized the "greenfield" Independence project despite substantial resistance from landowners in Ohio and Pennsylvania, who had recently argued that the new precedent agreements did not offer "adequate proof" of market backing. The agreements satisfied FERC's mandate for the projects to secure at least 35% of their total capacity from non-affiliated parties by June 26.

col0: One-way payment vs two-way payments in physical power and gas contracts It is my understanding that during the evolution of our physical power and natural gas markets, contract structures have grown increasingly sophisticated to reflect risk allocation and market volatility. In a one-way payment arrangement, the buyer pays the seller only if delivery occurs—typically at a pre-agreed price—while the seller bears the full risk of non-performance or curtailment. Conversely, two-way payment mechanisms require financial settlement in both directions: if actual deliveries deviate from scheduled volumes, either party compensates the other based on market-indexed rates. This symmetry better aligns incentives, encourages accurate scheduling, and mirrors the real-time balancing needs of grid operators. col3: FERC Authorizes Questar Pipeline Project The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has granted final approval for Questar's $155 million pipeline initiative to deliver natural gas from the Four Corners region—spanning New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, and Colorado—to southern California. This decision followed the commission's determination that the Questar Southern Trails Pipeline would pose no environmental threat. The project involves repurposing 693 miles of crude oil pipeline acquired by Questar from Arco in 1998, converting it for natural gas transport and constructing new compressors. It will be split into an East Zone, running from New Mexico's San Juan Basin to the California border with a capacity of 88 MMcf daily, and a West Zone within California, capable of moving 120 MMcf per day.

Research Approval Clarification  
Hi Sharad,  
Following our earlier discussion, I understand you've been requested to approve a calculation from another team—a task we occasionally encounter.  

In Research, we can evaluate a computation based on how well it meets its requirements, identify any limitations, and thus outline the risks involved in applying this approach. However, we cannot determine whether these risks are acceptable to Enron, as that decision clearly lies within RAC's domain.  

This leads to the question: Can Research actually approve anything for other groups? To "approve" implies acceptance, which our assessment alone cannot grant. It is more fitting for us to issue a technical note detailing the methodology, risks, and drawbacks of a method, while leaving the formal approval to those best positioned to evaluate these risks for the company. Otherwise, multiple departments might each form their own judgments on what constitutes acceptable risk for Enron.  

Steve

Its website functions as a digital storefront designed to facilitate product configuration and sales. Enron, by contrast, was an energy trading firm whose primary operations involved wholesale electricity and natural gas markets, not consumer-facing retail products. col0: To Our Readers: Here's the latest on Operation Enduring Freedom and the anthrax cases at home: In Afghanistan, the Pentagon is shifting its military policy toward more targeted strikes and increased reliance on local allies—a move that feels less like strategy and more like improvisation. Meanwhile, back in the States, the anthrax scare continues to fray nerves; every unopened envelope now carries a whisper of dread. It’s hard not to feel that we’re fighting shadows abroad while danger slips quietly through our own mail slots. The administration insists we’re safer, but safety feels fragile when fear spreads faster than facts. As journalists, we’re watching closely—not just troop movements or lab reports, but the quiet erosion of public trust. You deserve clarity, not just reassurance. We’ll keep digging, questioning, and reporting—because in times like these, truth isn’t just news; it’s armor. Stay vigilant, stay informed, and know we’re with you.

Responsibility for daily operations of building support services in the Enron Building, Houston leased offices, and Two Pacific Place (Omaha) will transition from Corporate to Enron Energy Services (EES) by year-end. The areas affected include facility operations and maintenance of mechanical, electrical, and air-conditioning systems; mail delivery; housekeeping; and food, copier, and records services.

This transition of services, currently managed by Enron Property and Services Corp. (EPSC), aims to optimize value for Enron's Business Units by utilizing facility management services now provided by EES to their commercial clients. EPSC staff with administrative duties for these services will report to Enron Facility Services, a subsidiary of EES's Global Energy Services group under Daniel Leff, President and CEO.

EPSC handles Enron's internal real estate and office development needs, including leasing, space allocation and facility planning, project and construction management, furniture systems, and office relocation. EPSC, in its development capacity, remains part of Enron Corporate Administration Services (ECAS) alongside Corporate Security and the Aviation Department, reporting to Bill Donovan, Vice President, Corporate Administrative Services.

This realignment allows EPSC to concentrate resources on efficiently using existing office space assets and overseeing the development of Houston's new Enron Center Campus project.

Though May has settled in with its lilac-scented breeze and daffodils bowing to warmer suns, I can’t help but linger in April’s echo—National Poetry Month. Remember how rain tapped sonnets on windowpanes? How dogwoods bloomed like stanzas unfurling? In quiet corners of libraries and coffee shops, strangers traded verses like sacred coins, eyes bright with shared rhythm. Even the wind seemed to recite Dickinson.  

Now, as spring deepens, let’s carry that lyric grace forward—not just in designated months, but in grocery lines, subway rides, midnight thoughts. Poetry isn’t confined to calendars; it lives where we dare to feel deeply.
